title: Tests are executable claims
summary: Use a log parser to turn requirements into falsifiable examples, boundary tests, and an evidence record.
objectives: Write a behavioral contract before implementing a parser
Separate corruption, incomplete input and I/O failure
Choose assertions that detect a meaningful regression
Use failing tests to narrow a hypothesis rather than edit at random
body:
Purpose: make a storage claim observable

A program can compile, print a plausible result, and still lose information after restart. The purpose of this lesson is to replace “it works” with a smaller claim that an experiment can challenge. Our subject is the replay function in P06. It consumes records and reconstructs a key map. Its contract distinguishes an empty stream, validated records, an incomplete declared header or payload, detected framing or checksum violations, and an actual read error. These parser categories do not identify every physical cause: bounded length damage can make an originally complete record appear incomplete. These are different observations with different consequences. Write those categories in your notebook before opening the implementation. A test is useful when you can name the requirement it would catch someone violating.

Model: arrange a state, perform one action, inspect evidence

Most tests have an arrangement, an action, and assertions. Arrangement constructs a known input without depending on yesterday's filesystem. The action crosses the boundary being tested. Assertions describe externally meaningful behavior. For a replay parser, asserting the number of recovered records is insufficient: a broken parser might count a damaged record and still return the right number. Check the recovered values and the valid byte boundary. A unit test can isolate decoding; an integration test can verify that opening a real file actually truncates a torn tail before appending. Neither observation alone establishes resistance to sudden power loss.

Predict before running

Imagine a valid record for key a followed by the first two bytes of a second record. Predict the recovered map, record count, valid byte offset and torn-tail flag. Now change the last byte of a complete record. Should this be treated as a harmless tail? Commit your answer before executing anything. The reference rejects a complete checksum mismatch because silently discarding it would hide corruption. A partial record has an unavoidable ambiguity: it might be an interrupted append or a damaged file that only resembles one. Recovery policy must state that assumption instead of claiming perfect diagnosis.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv every_torn_suffix
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv checksum_mismatch_with_complete_declared_payload
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv read_error

Read the runnable example

Find the test named every_torn_suffix_recovers_only_the_complete_prefix. The first encoded record remains intact. The loop varies every nonempty incomplete prefix of the second record. Concatenation creates a new input for each cut, replay interprets it, and assertions compare the valid prefix length with the first record's actual encoded length. This avoids a fragile handwritten offset. The range excludes a complete second record, which should have different expected behavior. Next read crc_known_vector: an independently known CRC value helps catch an encoder and decoder that agree only because they share the same wrong algorithm.

Intentional failure and guided checkpoint

In your working copy, temporarily change replay's checksum mismatch branch into a successful return. Run only the complete-declared-payload checksum-mismatch test and preserve the failure message. This is a small mutation experiment: it asks whether your test suite detects a specific defect. Restore the branch immediately afterward. Then implement the miniature parser in scaffolds/p06-kv. Its byte-sum checksum is intentionally simpler than KV01's CRC. Keep its format separate in your notes. The checkpoint is not copying the reference parser; it is explaining why a length must be validated before a slice or allocation and why a zero-length payload can still be a complete record.

mise exec -- cargo test --manifest-path scaffolds/p06-kv/Cargo.toml

Playbook investigation: the last value disappeared

Observation: a supplied file recovers one key, while a teammate expected two. Guess A says the replay loop stops too early. Guess B says the second append never formed a complete record. Guess C says a complete record failed its checksum. First record file length and the expected record boundaries. Then replay an in-memory concatenation of two independently encoded complete records. If both appear, that experiment disproves the broad claim that replay always stops after one record. Truncate the second record at several offsets and compare the recovered boundary. Finally flip one payload bit in a complete record. Each experiment changes one factor and produces a different predicted outcome.

A useful fix report names the observed failure class and the precise branch changed. It includes the smallest failing input, the old and new result, and the regression test. Its limitation statement says that synthetic truncation does not simulate every filesystem ordering or device failure. Avoid “all edge cases covered.” A finite suite covers the cases it contains and supports a reasoned argument about nearby cases. Keep the competing hypotheses, including the one disproved, in the investigation record.

Independent practice and tiered hints

Add an input reader that returns Interrupted once and then returns ordinary data. Decide whether replay should fail, retry, or discard a tail. Add a separate reader that returns an ordinary error halfway through a header. The two readers should not have identical expected results.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

inspect read_prefix rather than the CRC function.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

EOF is represented by a successful zero-byte read; an error is another variant.

Worked solution

Solution outline: retry Interrupted without increasing the used count, propagate other errors, and classify only actual EOF after a prefix as an incomplete tail. Keep the full answer folded in your notes until your own test exists.

Solution reasoning

The retry loop owns used, so a transient interruption preserves both buffer contents and position. A successful read advances used by its reported size. Returning an ordinary error keeps permission failures and device failures visible. Treating every error as EOF would silently reinterpret infrastructure failures as recoverable storage tails.

When you get stuck

Run one named test with -- --nocapture, inspect the assertion's left and right values, and draw byte offsets on paper. Read the standard Read documentation for the distinction between zero bytes and an error. Ask for review with the exact input bytes, command, expected result, actual result and smallest changed function. “The storage tests fail” does not identify an experiment another person can reproduce.

Reconstruct the complete early checkpoint

This complete early checkpoint replays a bounded miniature byte-sum format, preserving valid-prefix evidence. It is not the KV01/CRC32 format or a durable file store. The checkpoint contract and source are separately preserved. From the course root, run:

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p06 01-prefix-replay
cd learner-work/checkpoints/p06-kv/01-prefix-replay
mise exec -- cargo test
mise exec -- cargo run

The helper refuses an existing destination; choose a new explicit destination if you already have work there. This is a complete guided comparison checkpoint, not evidence that you independently implemented the project. Make predictions, inspect each boundary test, then carry the next requirement into your own source. A separately named final checkpoint reconstructs the current complete reference without pretending it is this earlier milestone. Exact reconstruction and test commands are recorded in the author check log.

Review, evidence and mastery

Submit a contract table, one detected mutation, the interruption test and a brief investigation log. Explain one test that would still pass under a plausible bug, then strengthen it. You are ready to continue when you can distinguish test evidence from a durability guarantee, predict a failure before running it, and make a regression test smaller without removing the behavior that triggers it.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Current scope and invariants. One cooperating writer owns the separate lock; only a validated record changes the map or recovery boundary. A failed write leaves the last acknowledged map readable and blocks further mutations until reopen.

Why this is the current recommended shape. A small binary protocol and BTreeMap keep framing and replay visible. Bounds precede allocation, typed io::Result values preserve failures, and owned File handles tie cleanup to scope. write_all and sync_all precede acknowledgment; compaction uses a separate lock inode and replaces the active data handle.

Reasonable alternative and tradeoff. An embedded database would provide a broader tested storage contract and should be preferred when a real application needs transactions, indexing, migrations or concurrent readers. This implementation is appropriate for learning one explicit single-writer log protocol; adding a framework would conceal the decisions being studied.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. CRC known vector; every truncated suffix of the tested record; checksum mismatch after a complete declared payload; invalid length; read failure; tombstones and empty values; tail repair; lock retention across compaction. Additional self-review regressions cover write-error poisoning and stale temporary files. The live map grows with the data set. CRC is not authentication. A bounded damaged length can resemble a torn tail and cause truncation of an originally complete record; the interrupted-append policy assumes earlier valid bytes were not damaged. Sync/rename tests do not reproduce every power-loss ordering. Unix compaction and cooperating advisory locks are explicit scope limits.

Requirement that would justify evolution. Adopt or evaluate an established storage engine when the requirements include multi-key atomicity, large state, coordinated concurrent readers or portable power-loss guarantees. Do not grow the current log by silently adding assumptions.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

Patch verification: the coordinated targeted suite passed after adding P06 write-failure and stale-compaction regressions and making P12 accounting private. The exact execution is recorded in verification/patch001-targeted.log; independent review remains pending.

title: Resource ownership and the failure path
summary: Use ownership, scopes, Drop and explicit synchronization to control file and lock lifetimes.
objectives: Trace who owns a file and its advisory lock
Distinguish automatic cleanup from successful persistence
Explain why a failed write poisons further mutation
Read a borrow-checker error as a lifetime conflict
body:
Purpose: reason about resources on every exit

A resource is more than allocated memory. A file descriptor, a lock, a worker handle and an initialized value all need a clear owner and an end to their lifetime. Rust associates cleanup with ownership: when a value is dropped, its destructor can release what it owns. This pattern makes early returns through the question-mark operator easier to reason about. It does not make every cleanup operation successful, and it does not replace explicit error handling. Our storage project makes that distinction concrete by owning both a data file and a separate lock file inside Store.

Model: scope boundaries carry cleanup, results carry failure

Consider opening a file and then failing to parse its contents. The local File still drops during the early return, so the descriptor does not need a manual close on every branch. A Store that opens successfully carries its lock until the Store drops. However, File's destructor cannot return a Result to the caller. If your requirement includes observing synchronization failure, call sync_all while you can still handle its result. A scope ending tells you when cleanup is attempted; it does not prove that bytes survived a machine crash. Draw these as separate arrows in your ownership diagram.

Predict the lock lifetime

Open a Store, try to open a second Store for the same path, then explicitly drop the first before trying again. Predict which attempt succeeds. Now imagine compaction replaces the data file using rename. If the advisory lock belonged only to the old data-file inode, could another process lock the new file? The reference keeps a separate persistent .lock file for precisely this reason. All cooperating writers must follow that convention. An advisory lock is not permission enforcement against an unrelated program that ignores the protocol or removes the lock file.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv reopen_repairs_tail
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv compaction_preserves_state
mise exec -- rustc --edition=2024 ../exercises/systems/borrow_after_pop.rs

The last command intentionally fails with E0502. It borrows the queue's first element, mutates the queue by popping, and then uses the old reference. The compiler refuses overlapping requirements for a shared reference and a mutable operation. It is preventing a reference from outliving the element that justified it. Decide whether the caller actually needs an owned String, a shorter borrow, or a different order of operations before reaching for clone.

Read the ownership decisions in the code

In Store::open, path is owned so later compaction does not depend on a caller's temporary path buffer. The _lock field looks unused to a calculation but is used by its lifetime. The file field receives a File opened for append. entries owns the latest values independently of the on-disk file. In change, encode runs before any I/O, so invalid arguments cannot partially append. write_all and sync_all finish before the map is changed. If either returns an error, poisoned becomes true, and later mutations return an error requiring the caller to reopen.

Why poison a resource that still exists?

After a failed write, the bytes on disk may include none, some, or all of the requested record. After a failed synchronization call, the visible file might contain a complete record while its durable status remains uncertain. The in-memory map intentionally stays at the last acknowledged state. Appending another record through the same object could create a valid record after an incomplete one, which the replay policy cannot safely interpret. Poisoning is a state-machine decision: further writes are prohibited until replay determines a valid prefix. Reads still show the last acknowledged in-memory state; they are not a definitive statement about what a later reopen will recover.

Playbook investigation: a lock seems stuck

Observation: a second open returns an error. Hypothesis A says the lock file's mere existence blocks all future use. Hypothesis B says an existing Store still owns an operating-system lock. Hypothesis C says the parent directory permissions prevent opening either file. Record the actual error and run a same-process test with an explicit drop between opens. If reopening succeeds while the .lock file remains, that disproves hypothesis A. Try a distinct writable temporary directory to separate permission problems from lock ownership. Do not “fix” the symptom by deleting the lock file while a writer may still hold it; that can split the locking protocol across different inodes.

A defensible fix shortens the unintended owner's scope or removes an unnecessary extra owner. Its evidence includes the failed second open, successful open after drop, and successful lock exclusion after compaction. Its limits include cooperating-writer assumptions and filesystem support. Avoid diagnosing every open error as contention: preserve enough error information to distinguish the categories. When an experiment disproves a guess, record that result rather than quietly replacing the guess with another story.

Guided checkpoint and independent practice

Draw the ownership graph before and after Store::open returns. Mark which resources clean up if replay fails. Then repair borrow_after_pop in two ways: one that moves the String out with pop_front, and one that limits the shared borrow to a smaller scope before mutation. Explain which version matches a caller that needs to keep the removed value. Independently design a small guard that increments an active-operation counter when created and decrements it on Drop. Test an early return and a panic caught with catch_unwind. Do not claim that destructors run after process abort, forced termination or power loss.

Tiered hints and solution reasoning
Hint 1: choose the next observation

the queue already exposes an ownership-transferring operation.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

Option<String> owns its contents while Option<&String> borrows.

Worked solution

A direct solution binds the result of pop_front and uses that owned value. For the counter guard, initialize the counter before constructing the guard and put only the decrement in Drop; do not use a destructor as the place to report a fallible business operation.

When you get stuck

Run the intentional compiler failure alone and underline the first borrow, the mutation, and the later use. Read File's Drop and sync_all documentation. For a runtime issue, add a minimal scope boundary and rerun the lock test before changing locking code. Ask for review with an ownership sketch and the exact error kind; include whether the first Store has actually dropped.

Review and mastery evidence

Submit the ownership graph, both borrow-error repairs, and the guard experiment. Explain why automatic cleanup simplifies control flow but does not guarantee successful persistence. You have mastered this lesson when you can locate the owner responsible for cleanup, identify fallible work that must occur before Drop, and state what the program knows and does not know after a write failure.

title: Design an append-only record protocol
summary: Implement bounded binary records, exact checksums, tombstones and replayable state transitions.
objectives: Derive a record layout with explicit integer widths and endianness
Reject untrusted lengths before allocating
Distinguish empty values from deletions
Explain acknowledgment order and uncertain write outcomes
body:
Purpose: let a process reconstruct its past

An in-memory map forgets everything when the process ends. The first storage design we will study records operations as an append-only sequence. A put records a key and value; a delete records a key and a deletion marker. Restart replays operations in order to reconstruct the latest map. This is intentionally a small single-writer design. It has no transactions across multiple keys, no multi-process reader snapshots, no indexes on disk, and no replication. Those omissions keep the state transitions visible enough to reason about rather than hiding them behind a database library.

Model: format bytes are a public contract

A KV01 record starts with four magic bytes, a little-endian 32-bit key length, a little-endian 32-bit value length, and a 32-bit CRC. Payload bytes follow: key first, then value. The reserved value length u32::MAX means deletion; a length of zero means a present empty value. Key lengths are one through 4096, and values have a one-megabyte maximum. The decoder checks those limits before allocating a payload. Integer widths and byte order are explicit because a file may outlive the compiler process that produced it. A native-memory representation is not a stable file format.

Prediction and runnable example

Predict the map after put a=old, put a=new, put b=temporary, delete b. The log has four records while the map has one live key. Predict what changes if the second put stores an empty value. The key remains present because an empty value is distinct from deletion. Use a path inside your project directory so you know exactly which files this exercise creates. Repeating these commands appends more records; replay still selects the latest operation for each key.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo run -p p06-kv -- lesson-store.kv put a old
mise exec -- cargo run -p p06-kv -- lesson-store.kv put a new
mise exec -- cargo run -p p06-kv -- lesson-store.kv put b temporary
mise exec -- cargo run -p p06-kv -- lesson-store.kv delete b
mise exec -- cargo run -p p06-kv -- lesson-store.kv get a
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv overwritten_deleted_and_empty_values

Trace the implementation one decision at a time

encode checks caller-supplied lengths, writes fixed-width header fields, inserts a temporary checksum field and appends payload. The checksum covers the first twelve header bytes and the payload, excluding its own field. Including lengths helps detect accidental header damage only when the declared payload can be read completely; the CRC is checked after that read. replay reads the fixed header, checks the magic, interprets deletion, rejects invalid lengths, and only then allocates bounded payload storage. After a complete payload and matching checksum, it updates the map and advances valid_bytes. Those two actions happen together at the end of successful decoding so a partially read record never moves the recovery boundary.

Checksums are evidence with a scope

CRC-32 is an error-detection mechanism for accidental damage. It is not cryptographic authentication, and different byte sequences can share a CRC. The reference has a known-vector test using 123456789, then tests corrupted records. That combination is more informative than simply encoding and decoding with the same code. A checksum mismatch after reading the complete declared payload is a hard error, even at the end of the file. This is narrower than rejecting all corruption of an originally complete record. The parser never scans ahead for another magic string after damage: a magic pattern could occur inside an ordinary key or value, making such recovery ambiguous without a stronger framing protocol.

Acknowledgment order is part of the API

Store::change encodes before writing, calls write_all, calls sync_all, and then changes the in-memory map. The caller receives success only after those steps. write_all handles short successful writes by retrying, but it may still return an error after a prefix was written. A synchronization error can likewise leave an uncertain outcome. The object refuses later writes until reopened. A caller cannot assume that an error means the operation definitely did not occur on disk. This is why higher-level protocols often need operation identifiers and idempotency rules; a local Result alone cannot erase uncertainty introduced by I/O.

Intentional failure and guided checkpoint

Change a copy of the decoder to allocate using the declared key length before checking MAX_KEY. Do not feed it an enormous real allocation. Instead inspect the ordering and write a test that supplies an invalid declared length with no payload. The correct decoder returns InvalidData before requesting that payload. Restore the correct order. Your checkpoint is to describe the validation sequence without reading the implementation: header completeness, magic, bounded lengths, payload completeness, checksum, then map mutation. Explain why changing that order can turn malformed input into excessive allocation or partially accepted state.

Playbook investigation: empty value or missing key?

Observation: get produces an empty byte slice for one key while another key is absent. Hypothesis A says both are deletions. Hypothesis B says one is an empty put and the other a tombstone. Hypothesis C says replay ignored a damaged record. Inspect the value-length field for each record and run the overwritten/deleted/empty-values test. Construct a complete empty-value record with a valid CRC; if it remains in the map, that disproves hypothesis A. Then flip a checksum byte and confirm an error rather than a missing key. This experiment separates encoding semantics from the command-line renderer's presentation.

A fix may belong in display formatting rather than storage. Record whether the incorrect observation came from the map, encoded bytes, or human-readable output. Evidence should include a contains/get distinction and the format bytes. Its limits include CRC collisions and the single-writer assumption. Do not expand this result into a claim that the store can recover arbitrary corruption or safely accept hostile concurrent file modification.

Independent practice, hints and review

Add a pure inspection function that reports record offsets and operation kinds without exposing value contents. Keep bounded lengths and the same corruption policy.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

reuse decoding decisions, not the CLI's lossy text formatting.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

every reported offset must be a validated boundary.

Worked solution

Solution direction: factor one-record decoding into a result that distinguishes clean EOF, torn tail and a validated operation, then let replay and inspection consume that result. Preserve all existing failure tests and add an offset test containing an empty value and a deletion.

When you get stuck

Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv crc_known_vector, then the single test matching your failure category. Draw one sixteen-byte header with each field labeled. Read u32::from_le_bytes and Write::write_all documentation. Ask for review with the exact bytes and intended semantic operation; a screenshot of a map alone cannot show a framing error.

Evidence and mastery

Submit your record diagram, the offset inspector's tests, and an explanation of one rejected alternative format. You are ready to proceed when you can decode a record by hand, distinguish deletion from empty data, and explain why successful synchronization and publication of in-memory state occur in that order.

A framing counterexample worth keeping

A complete put of key a and value one declares a value length of 3. Change that field to 4 in a disposable copy without changing the file length. The new length is legal, but the decoder now expects a byte that is absent. It reports torn_tail before checking the CRC. Store::open then truncates to the previous validated boundary. Even though the original put was acknowledged, later length damage can cause its removal. The test below deliberately preserves this counterexample so the course cannot quietly overstate the format's guarantee.

mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv --test persistence_edges bounded_length_damage

Predict how this differs from flipping one payload bit without changing lengths. Explain when CRC can be evaluated in each case. For unknown real damage, preserve the original bytes before opening a copy for inspection. A future format with independently checked framing needs its own version and migration tests; CRC would still not provide authentication or eliminate collisions.

title: Recovery and compaction without wishful guarantees
summary: Specify restart policy, test torn tails, and reason through compaction failure windows.
objectives: Distinguish a valid prefix from arbitrary damaged data
Explain truncate-before-append recovery
Trace write/sync/rename/directory-sync ordering
State filesystem and power-loss limits precisely
body:
Purpose: make restarting part of normal behavior

Durability is not a property you earn by adding one sync call. It is a protocol whose states include interruption. This lesson treats restart as a normal entry point and asks what the program can infer from each file shape. Recovery accepts a sequence of complete validated records and may discard an incomplete final record. A full header with bad magic or out-of-range lengths produces an error; a checksum mismatch produces an error only after the declared payload is fully available. This is a conservative policy: it avoids silently treating identifiable corruption as a successful recovery. Its recovery guarantee assumes an interrupted append following unchanged valid prior records. It cannot distinguish every form of damage from interruption.

Model: a validated prefix plus an uncertain suffix

During replay, valid_bytes advances only after a complete record has passed validation and affected the map. If the final header or payload ends early, replay returns that earlier boundary with torn_tail=true. Store::open truncates the file to that boundary and synchronizes it before allowing another append. Without truncation, a new valid record would follow the old incomplete bytes. A later replay could interpret those bytes together as one malformed record and lose access to the later append. Recovery is therefore not merely ignoring data in memory; it repairs the on-disk suffix before normal operation resumes.

Predict two interruption outcomes

Suppose the first record is intact and the next record is missing three payload bytes. Predict the recovered key set and resulting file length after open. Now suppose the second record is complete but one payload bit changed. The first case repairs an incomplete suffix; the second refuses to open. Explain why treating both as “last record bad, ignore it” would hide damage. Then predict whether deleting an old key reduces the log size. It does not: deletion adds a tombstone. Reclaiming historical records requires a separate compaction protocol.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv every_torn_suffix
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv reopen_repairs_tail
mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv compaction_preserves_state
mise exec -- cargo run -p p06-kv -- lesson-store.kv compact

The compaction command is implemented for Unix platforms, including the course's macOS environment. It operates on a store you created in the prior lesson. Do not treat its platform guard as a claim that all Unix filesystems and storage devices provide identical persistence guarantees.

Read the compaction protocol

compact creates a sibling temporary file with create_new, writes one current put per live key, synchronizes the new file, renames it over the old data path, swaps the Store's open file handle, and synchronizes the containing directory. Keeping the temporary file in the same directory avoids an intended cross-filesystem move. The original lock uses a different inode, so it remains held across replacement. The new handle must replace the old handle: otherwise subsequent appends could go to the unlinked old file while new opens read the compacted file.

Failure windows deserve a table

Before rename, the original data path remains the authoritative log. A write or sync failure while constructing the temporary file may leave that temporary file behind. create_new deliberately refuses to overwrite an existing .compact file on the next attempt. Inspect and remove a stale temporary file only while no writer owns the store, after deciding which data path is authoritative. After rename, the current process points at the new file. If directory synchronization fails, namespace persistence across a crash is uncertain and the Store becomes poisoned. Reopening and inspecting is necessary; pretending that the failed call rolled the rename back would be wrong.

File synchronization asks the operating system to synchronize file data and relevant metadata. Synchronizing a directory after rename is the Unix protocol used here to address the directory-entry change. The exact persistence outcome still depends on filesystem, operating system, mount options and hardware behavior. Unit tests that truncate a file or flip bytes model parser inputs; they do not emulate every ordering of device writes. State those limits in the project's evidence record. Use “tested recovery from these constructed tails” rather than “crash-proof.”

Playbook investigation: new writes vanish after compaction

Observation: get succeeds in the existing process after compaction and a put, but reopening does not show that put. Hypothesis A says replay mishandles the new record. Hypothesis B says writes still target the old open file handle. Hypothesis C says compaction omitted an older key. Keep the test data small: put a, compact, put b, drop, reopen, inspect both. Then compare the path's file length before and after the second put. A map change without growth at the visible path supports B. Replay an explicitly concatenated compacted record plus b in memory; success disproves the broad parser hypothesis.

The corresponding fix is to replace the Store's file handle after rename while retaining the independent lock. Evidence includes reopening after an additional append, the resulting map, and a contention check after compaction. It does not prove every crash window is safe. For an advanced extension, introduce explicit failure points into a filesystem adapter and test the selected authoritative file after each one. Keep injection semantics honest: an injected error before rename is not evidence about an actual power loss during rename.

Guided checkpoint and independent practice

Write a six-row failure table covering temporary creation, record write, file sync, rename, handle replacement and directory sync. For every row state which path is authoritative, which resources remain open and whether another mutation is allowed. Independently add a test where .compact already exists. The expected outcome is a visible error while the original log remains usable.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

choose create_new rather than check-then-create.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

successful compaction must never depend on deleting a file whose provenance is unknown.

Worked solution

Solution direction: retain the old Store until the new file is ready and make incomplete cleanup an explicit operational condition.

When you get stuck

Run the reopen-and-append test first. Inspect file lengths and record boundaries rather than adding random sleeps. Read File::sync_all and std::fs::rename's platform notes. Ask for review with your failure-window table, exact interruption point, and observations from both the live process and a reopened Store. Distinguish “the call returned an error” from “the operation definitely did not occur.”

Review, evidence and mastery

Submit the failure table, stale-temporary test and a restart trace. You have mastered the lesson when you can explain why a repaired tail must be truncated, why a renamed file needs a new active handle, and what remains uncertain after each failed synchronization. A good answer identifies the limits of the experiment as precisely as its successful outcome.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Current scope and invariants. One cooperating writer owns the separate lock; only a validated record changes the map or recovery boundary. A failed write leaves the last acknowledged map readable and blocks further mutations until reopen.

Why this is the current recommended shape. A small binary protocol and BTreeMap keep framing and replay visible. Bounds precede allocation, typed io::Result values preserve failures, and owned File handles tie cleanup to scope. write_all and sync_all precede acknowledgment; compaction uses a separate lock inode and replaces the active data handle.

Reasonable alternative and tradeoff. An embedded database would provide a broader tested storage contract and should be preferred when a real application needs transactions, indexing, migrations or concurrent readers. This implementation is appropriate for learning one explicit single-writer log protocol; adding a framework would conceal the decisions being studied.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. CRC known vector; every truncated suffix of the tested record; checksum mismatch after a complete declared payload; invalid length; read failure; tombstones and empty values; tail repair; lock retention across compaction. Additional self-review regressions cover write-error poisoning and stale temporary files. The live map grows with the data set. CRC is not authentication. A bounded damaged length can resemble a torn tail and cause truncation of an originally complete record; the interrupted-append policy assumes earlier valid bytes were not damaged. Sync/rename tests do not reproduce every power-loss ordering. Unix compaction and cooperating advisory locks are explicit scope limits.

Requirement that would justify evolution. Adopt or evaluate an established storage engine when the requirements include multi-key atomicity, large state, coordinated concurrent readers or portable power-loss guarantees. Do not grow the current log by silently adding assumptions.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

Patch verification: the coordinated targeted suite passed after adding P06 write-failure and stale-compaction regressions and making P12 accounting private. The exact execution is recorded in verification/patch001-targeted.log; independent review remains pending.

Keep path identity stable across the operation

Store::open now uses std::path::absolute before opening either the lock or data file. It records the opening current directory in an absolute path, returning an io::Error if resolving a relative path fails. Later compaction therefore uses the same pathname even if the process changes directories. This is not canonicalization: symlinks are not resolved, and an external rename, symlink retargeting, or another pathname alias can still defeat assumptions. Cooperating writers must use the same stable data and lock paths.

Our isolated child-process regression opens data in one directory, writes a, changes its directory, compacts, writes b, and reopens the original data path. Before this fix b disappeared from that reopened path because compaction created a second file in the new directory. The test now requires both keys to survive and no second data file to appear. Only the child changes its process-wide current directory; the parallel test runner remains untouched. Hypothesis A, a decoder error, is disproved by reading the two physical files. Hypothesis B, pathname interpretation changing over time, predicts exactly that split.

mise exec -- cargo test -p p06-kv --test persistence_edges relative_store

The existing stale-temporary regression also checks that a refused .compact file retains its original bytes. The store uses create_new and never deletes an unknown temporary file for the caller. These tests establish pathname and file-ownership behavior under the modeled operations; they do not simulate external directory interference or power loss.

Recovery cannot infer the cause of every short payload

Run the bounded_length_damage test from the prior lesson and compare its bytes with a truly interrupted append. KV01 has no independent header checksum, so a legal length changed from 3 to 4 can make a previously complete record look incomplete and eligible for truncation. Do not summarize this policy as rejecting all complete corruption. When the cause is uncertain, preserve the original file, inspect a copy, and document which records would be discarded before authorizing a real recovery.

Investigate the command boundary before opening storage

A rejected command must not create a database or repair its existing tail. Opening this particular store is a state-changing operation: Store::open can truncate an incomplete suffix. The CLI therefore first checks the complete command, its exact argument count, UTF-8 text fields, and byte-length limits. Only then does it open the native PathBuf. The small Command enum carries borrowed validated bytes; it adds no shared ownership or copies of key/value data.

Prediction: run an unknown command against a disposable file containing only KV. Should its two bytes remain? The regression initially observed unwanted file creation before validation; the corrected process-level test checks both a missing path and an existing torn file, including absence of a new lock file. This disproves the tempting hypothesis that a nonzero exit status alone establishes that nothing changed. Inspect tests/cli.rs, then execute mise exec -- cargo test --manifest-path projects/Cargo.toml -p p06-kv --test cli from the course root.

Paths are operating-system values, while this CLI's keys and values are UTF-8 text. args_os preserves that distinction and to_str reports a text conversion failure. A native filename need not have a valid string representation; the host filesystem can also reject a name. On the author machine, a non-UTF-8 directory name produced a normal filesystem error rather than a panic; valid Unicode directory and file operations round-tripped. Library callers may store binary values, so CLI output uses lossy display only after reading, never to select or rewrite a path. A successful get can still repair a torn store because that is the declared open policy. It is not a forensic read-only inspector.

When stuck, first separate argument rejection from failure inside Store::open; preserve original bytes before investigating recovery. Add one rejected input to the regression and explain why it must be checked before opening. See the executed CLI boundary evidence and Rust 1.99 argument contract.

Output is an I/O boundary too. The CLI writes through a locked io::Write handle and propagates ordinary stdout failures, including a pipe whose consumer has closed. Final stderr diagnostics are best effort: a second write failure must not replace the original failure with a panic. The process tests create an anonymous pipe and close its reading end before launching the child, so this experiment does not depend on a race with a shell command.

A recovery warning is also best effort: the store may already have repaired its tail, and a broken stderr cannot undo that authorized operation. The test verifies this policy separately from rejecting an invalid command before opening.

title: Ownership crosses thread boundaries
summary: Build a bounded producer–worker–collector pipeline while preserving ownership and termination.
objectives: Explain Send and shared ownership without assuming Arc makes all data thread-safe
Keep lock scopes smaller than the work they coordinate
Trace channel closure and scoped-thread completion
Distinguish scheduling variation from result semantics
body:
Purpose: overlap independent work without losing control

Indexing several files gives us naturally independent tasks. Each worker can own one path, open one file, calculate a result, and send that result to a collector. The challenge is not merely spawning threads. It is knowing who owns each job, how many jobs can wait, who receives each result, and how every participant terminates. P07 uses a producer, a bounded job channel, a fixed set of workers, a bounded result channel and one collector. Before reading the code, draw those five parts and mark the direction in which ownership moves.

Model: transfer ownership or synchronize shared access

A channel send transfers an owned value to a receiver. After sending a PathBuf, the sender cannot keep using that moved value unless it created another owned copy. Send describes whether ownership can cross a thread boundary. Sync describes whether references can be shared safely across threads. Arc provides atomic shared ownership, but it does not make arbitrary interior operations safe; the contained type still determines what access is permitted. The receiver in this example is protected by a Mutex because multiple workers need to call its single-consumer receive operation in a coordinated way.

Predict compiler failures before repairing them

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- rustc --edition=2024 ../exercises/systems/rc_thread.rs
mise exec -- rustc --edition=2024 ../exercises/systems/thread_borrow.rs
mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer queue_one

The first command intentionally fails with E0277 because Rc's non-atomic ownership bookkeeping is not suitable for this transfer. The second intentionally fails with E0373 because an ordinary spawned thread could outlive the local String it borrows. Predict which failure can be repaired with move and which needs a different ownership mechanism. Do not solve both by adding Arc everywhere. A value used by only one worker can simply be moved. A scoped thread can borrow a local value when the enclosing scope guarantees the thread completes before the borrowed value leaves its scope.

Trace the actual pipeline

The input batch is validated before threads start. The producer enumerates paths and sends an input index with each path. Worker clones share access to the receiver and cancellation flag, while each result sender is an independent channel handle. Within a worker, the mutex guard exists only long enough to receive a job. The guard is dropped before count opens and reads the file. That narrow scope matters: keeping the guard through the file read would serialize most useful work even though several threads exist. Active-worker statistics surround counting, not waiting to send the finished result.

Bounded channels create backpressure

A bounded channel can make send wait when its buffer is full. That is useful because the producer cannot create an unlimited backlog. It also makes the dependency graph important. If the parent tried to produce every job before receiving results, workers could block on a full result queue while the producer blocked on a full job queue. No participant would make progress. P07 runs the producer in its own scoped thread and lets the parent drain results concurrently. The queue-one test uses many jobs to exercise this interaction with little spare buffering.

Channel termination depends on ownership of handles. Receivers learn that a channel is disconnected only when every sender is gone. The parent drops its unused result sender before collecting. Workers eventually drop their clones when no jobs remain or cancellation is observed. The producer drops the job sender on exit. thread::scope ensures the spawned thread bodies are joined before its call finishes. This means references to local statistics stay valid for the workers' operation. A panic in a worker is still a failure; scoped threads do not make panics disappear or convert them automatically into ordinary per-file results.

Playbook investigation: four workers behave like one

Observation: a run reports a peak active count of one. Hypothesis A says the machine has only one usable CPU. Hypothesis B says file reading occurs while the receiver mutex remains held. Hypothesis C says the chosen files are too small for overlap to appear. Select two experiments before editing. Inspect the lexical lifetime of the guard, then compare tiny files with larger ordinary files while holding configuration fixed. A correct guard scope and occasional peak above one on larger inputs disproves “the program always serializes all work.” A synthetic delayed counting function can isolate coordination from disk behavior, but its timing is not a disk-performance measurement.

A justified fix may shorten a guard lifetime; it may also be no code change if the observation came from an uninformative workload. Report the hypothesis, predicted outcome and result. Do not introduce sleep into production code to make the peak statistic look better. A higher peak is not automatically higher throughput: storage contention and scheduling overhead can make extra workers slower.

Guided checkpoint and independent practice

Mark every send, receive and drop in the pipeline diagram. Explain why the collector eventually sees channel closure on the ordinary path. Then repair the two compile-fail examples using ownership that matches the task. Independently write a two-worker pipeline with a queue capacity of one and a finite set of integer jobs. Add an early producer exit and prove the collector terminates. Leave yourself the decision of whether a worker panic should terminate the whole batch or become a structured batch error; document the policy before implementation.

Tiered hints and solution reasoning
Hint 1: choose the next observation

count remaining sender handles, not just threads.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

a temporary mutex guard lasts through its expression or explicit binding scope.

Worked solution

For the Rc example, moving a plain String is sufficient when there is only one consumer; Arc is appropriate only when shared ownership is actually needed. For the local borrow, move ownership or use thread::scope. The reference pipeline's producer thread avoids waiting for all submissions before any collection can occur.

When you get stuck

Reduce to queue capacity one and two jobs, draw each participant's next blocking operation, and identify which handle keeps a channel open. Run the single queue-one test. Read sync_channel and thread::scope documentation. Ask for review with the dependency diagram, handle ownership and the exact point where progress stops; “Rust threads deadlock” is a hypothesis, not an observation.

Review and mastery

Submit the pipeline diagram, compiler-error repairs and a termination argument. You are ready when you can explain why each shared object needs its particular wrapper, predict a bounded-channel deadlock from ownership and waiting, and distinguish output correctness from nondeterministic completion order.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Current scope and invariants. At most the configured fixed number of workers count files, both channels are bounded, each file uses a fixed-size read buffer, and input paths plus collected results have explicit batch limits.

Why this is the current recommended shape. Owned jobs move through channels; Arc is used only for shared cancellation and receiver ownership. Mutex scope covers dequeue, not file I/O. A pure streaming counter preserves state across reads, per-file status preserves partial failures, and final sorting makes entries deterministic.

Reasonable alternative and tradeoff. A work-stealing library is a reasonable alternative for CPU-heavy independent jobs and may simplify scheduling. The explicit fixed worker pool is a good fit here because its bounded queues and shutdown dependencies are the subject and are small enough to inspect. Unbounded thread-per-file spawning is a deliberate rejected design, not an early recommended step.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. Chunk-boundary counts; empty files; oversize and missing paths; cancellation before submission; queue-one termination; repeatable entries; invalid configuration. The total bound includes capped path/result metadata, not just the 8192-byte buffers. Ordinary file reads can block cancellation. Files may change during a run. Partial counts from failed or oversized files are not complete-file statistics.

Requirement that would justify evolution. For recursive or effectively unbounded discovery, stream results to a sink and use bounded or external sorting instead of collecting an unlimited list. For hard shutdown deadlines, revisit the synchronous I/O boundary and supported file types.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

title: Bound memory and make concurrent results reproducible
summary: Complete a streaming file indexer with explicit resource limits, cooperative cancellation, live progress and stable final output.
objectives: Derive memory bounds across input, queues, workers and output
Keep streaming parser state across arbitrary read boundaries
Define cancellation as a cooperative protocol
Produce deterministic results despite nondeterministic scheduling
Report bounded live progress without treating failed or abandoned jobs as successful files
body:
Purpose: put a resource budget in the design

A worker count alone does not bound a program's memory. A producer might retain millions of paths, an unbounded queue might hold millions of jobs, a worker might read an entire huge file, and a collector might accumulate every result forever. P07 addresses each category. It accepts a finite batch capped at 4096 paths, caps each encoded path length, uses bounded channels, permits at most 32 workers, reads through an 8192-byte buffer, limits bytes read per file and collects at most one result per submitted path. This is a bounded-batch design, not a claim of constant total memory independent of input count.

Model: streaming state is smaller than streaming input

The counter tracks total bytes, newline count, word count, whether the previous byte was inside a word, the last byte seen, and a rolling fingerprint. Words use ASCII whitespace boundaries, which is an explicit definition rather than a Unicode linguistic tokenizer. A long word may span several reads; in_word carries its state across those reads. Lines count newline bytes plus one final unterminated nonempty line. An empty file has zero lines. The fingerprint helps compare results, but it is not cryptographic authentication and does not prove two files are identical.

Predict before running

Predict the line and word counts for an empty file, a single newline, “a b” without a trailing newline, and a nine-thousand-byte word followed by another word. Decide whether a read boundary creates a new word. It must not. Now predict the oversize result if the maximum is four bytes and the source yields five. File metadata is only a preliminary observation; the reader itself must enforce the budget because files can change and some readers have no reliable metadata. The implementation reads at most the remaining budget plus one byte so it can detect an excess.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo run -p p07-indexer -- reference/p07-indexer/src/lib.rs reference/p07-indexer/src/main.rs
mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer streaming_counts
mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer oversize
mise exec -- cargo test --manifest-path scaffolds/p07-indexer/Cargo.toml

Read the bounded path

Config validation occurs before spawning. count owns the path and produces one Entry, including an explicit Status. Opening a missing file becomes a per-file failure rather than aborting all valid files. TooLarge means counters and fingerprint are partial; callers should not display them as completed-file measurements. The read loop preserves word state and checks cancellation between reads. The result collector sorts by path and then original input index. That second key makes repeated paths deterministic too. Thread completion order may change between runs, but the sorted entries for unchanged files should remain equal.

Live progress: observations belong to the collector

A final report cannot tell someone whether a longer run is still making progress. The collector already receives one result for each returned file job, so it is the natural owner of progress counts. The new index_with_progress function takes an FnMut callback: a function-like value that can update its captured state each time it is called. The callback runs on the calling thread before workers start, after each received Entry, and once after all scoped work has joined and output has been sorted. It receives a small copied Progress value; no progress thread, shared counter lock, timer, or additional queue is needed. The existing index function calls the same implementation with a callback that does nothing, preserving the earlier API and benchmark's output-free measurement boundary.

Predict this snapshot: total=3, received=2, indexed=1, failed=1, finished=false. Have two files been indexed successfully? No. Two results arrived, but one is an error. Does the remaining file necessarily run now? No: it might still be queued. The equation received = indexed + too_large + failed + cancelled holds at every observation. Only the final snapshot supplies submitted, after joining the producer. Then submitted - received counts accepted jobs without a returned result, and total - submitted counts jobs never submitted. These are distinct from returned Status::Cancelled entries. Cancellation need not make received equal total, and the interface must not turn that gap into false success.

The callback receives at most total + 2 snapshots, with total capped at 4096. The indexer retains one progress value. A caller choosing to keep snapshots owns that additional bounded storage; the CLI prints each observation instead. Result-arrival order depends on scheduling, while each category count increases monotonically and the final entries remain sorted. A slow callback deliberately slows collection: the existing bounded result queue eventually blocks workers. Do not wait inside the callback for this same indexing run to finish; that would prevent the collector from doing the work required for completion. The callback has no hard deadline, and a blocked filesystem read can still postpone cancellation.

Guided checkpoint: keep status separate from data

Read the complete CLI below, then run it from the course projects directory. Compared with the previous thin entry point, it passes a retained cancellation flag and a small closure to index_with_progress. Progress goes to standard error; sorted entries and the final report go to standard output. The status writer uses Write and returns an ordinary I/O error. If progress output fails, the closure records that first error and requests cancellation. The indexer still drains returned results and joins scoped work, then the CLI returns the error without printing a successful report. A callback panic remains a programmer failure, not a normal output-error policy.

mise exec -- cargo run -p p07-indexer -- reference/p07-indexer/src/lib.rs reference/p07-indexer/src/main.rs
mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer progress_
mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer initial_progress
mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer --test cli

The first command prints a started observation at received=0/2, one running observation for each returned file, and a finished observation at received=2/2 when both files exist and fit their budgets. It also prints the sorted file results. The relative interleaving of the two terminal streams is not part of the contract. Progress is per returned file, not a byte-level timer: a single slow file may produce no intermediate line. The CLI does not install a Ctrl-C handler; library callers can set the retained cancellation flag, and the CLI does so if its progress sink fails.

Playbook: a cancelled run shows only one completed result

Observation: total=32, but received is much smaller after cancellation. Hypothesis A says the collector lost results. Hypothesis B says queued or not-yet-submitted jobs were stopped. A controlled experiment uses one worker, queue capacity one, and requests cancellation in the callback after the first received result. Run progress_cancellation_drains_results_and_accounts_for_unreturned_jobs. Its final snapshot agrees with every returned Entry, separates unreturned submitted jobs from unsubmitted jobs, and checks the conservation equation. This disproves the claim that received must always equal the original batch size. Exact intermediate counts are intentionally not hardcoded: scheduling can change which job crosses the boundary before the flag is seen.

Deliberate mistake to diagnose: display received/total as “files successfully indexed,” or add a shared mutable progress counter to every worker. The former mixes completion and success; the latter adds synchronization although the collector already owns the evidence. Correct the label and count Status::Indexed at collection. Independently add a quiet-progress CLI option without changing stdout or index results. Before coding, decide whether disabling progress changes how output failures are handled.

Progress hint 1

Trace one missing file. It contributes to received and failed, but not indexed. Trace one never-submitted job separately.

Progress hint 2

A callback capturing a Vec can record a test trace without being Send because the coordinator invokes it synchronously. Bound the test fixture and compare final categories with Report.entries.

Worked progress review

Keep index as a wrapper around index_with_progress. For a quiet option, select a no-output callback after validating arguments; preserve the same index and sort path. Test identical stdout with and without progress, and require that quiet mode does not claim to test a stderr write that never occurs. A background progress channel is justified only if an independently scheduled interface needs it, and that interface must choose a bounded queue or coalesced latest snapshot.

Evidence: the focused progress verification report records initial, monotonic, final, empty-input, invalid-configuration, cancellation, read-failure, and CLI output-failure checks. These tests support the callback contract and executed schedules. They do not measure throughput or establish every filesystem's shutdown timing. Mastery requires explaining why a finished cancelled run can have fewer results than inputs, demonstrating a distinguishing experiment, and defending the chosen observer boundary without reading this explanation.

Cancellation needs an honest boundary

The cancellation flag uses relaxed atomic operations because it is only a stop hint; it is not publishing some other protected data structure. A worker checks it before waiting for another job and between reads. Cancellation cannot forcibly interrupt a blocking regular-file read through this API. A special file or problematic filesystem may block longer than expected, so use ordinary local files in the course exercises. The producer may already have submitted a job when cancellation arrives. Therefore submitted, completed entries and canceled state can differ. Do not interpret submitted as a guaranteed number of completed indexes.

The producer and workers still have to close channels correctly. A canceled worker drops its receiver clone and result sender. Once all job receivers disappear, a blocked producer send returns an error. The collector drains finished results until all senders disappear, and the scope waits for thread completion. This protocol bounds outstanding work but does not promise a hard wall-clock shutdown deadline for synchronous file I/O. That limitation motivates the different I/O model in the next project.

Playbook investigation: word counts change with buffer size

Observation: a learner's indexer counts the same bytes differently with one-byte reads and eight-kilobyte reads. Hypothesis A says the operating system changes the file contents. Hypothesis B says the tokenizer resets in_word at every read. Hypothesis C says the final unterminated line is counted as a word. Choose a reader adapter that returns one byte per call while holding the underlying byte slice fixed. If the result still changes, that disproves the operating-system-content hypothesis without involving threads at all. Then use a single long word to separate boundary-state mistakes from line-ending logic.

The likely repair is to move parser state outside the read loop, but make that conclusion only after the minimal experiment. Evidence includes identical counts for several chunk sizes, empty input and trailing-newline cases. Its limits include the chosen ASCII word definition and concurrent external file edits. In the middle stage of the course, you choose which assertions distinguish your remaining hypotheses; the lesson no longer supplies every expected byte count.

Guided checkpoint and independent practice

Complete the scaffold's generic Read-based counter before adding concurrency. Its Tiny reader deliberately splits every token boundary. Then estimate memory as bounded input paths, queued paths, per-worker buffers, queued results and collected results. Include allocation overhead qualitatively; do not advertise the sum as an exact resident-set measurement. Independently add aggregate statistics for completed files only. Decide how duplicates and errors affect totals, write that policy, and test it before changing the CLI. Preserve deterministic entry order while allowing runtime peak-worker statistics to vary.

Tiered hints and solution reasoning
Hint 1: choose the next observation

read boundaries are transport events, not text delimiters.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

count a word only on a whitespace-to-nonwhitespace transition, with an initially false in_word.

Worked solution

Solution outline: preserve state across successful reads, retry Interrupted, return other errors, and account for the last line after genuine EOF. For totals, filter Status::Indexed explicitly; a partial TooLarge entry must not contribute as though the whole file had been read.

When you get stuck

Run the scaffold counter against Tiny before inspecting channels. Use mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer queue_one only after pure counting is correct. Read the Read contract and the sync_channel blocking behavior. Ask for review with the bytes, chunk sizes, cancellation timing and your resource-budget equation. Keep “bounded memory” separate from “fast” and “hard-deadline cancellation.”

Review, evidence and mastery

Submit streaming boundary tests, the memory budget, cancellation semantics and two identical sorted-output captures from unchanged inputs. You have mastered the project when you can identify every quantity that can grow, explain why a file failure remains visible without stopping unrelated work, and state which observations are deterministic and which depend on scheduling.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Current scope and invariants. At most the configured fixed number of workers count files, both channels are bounded, each file uses a fixed-size read buffer, and input paths plus collected results have explicit batch limits. Live progress uses one coordinator-owned value and no new channel; received results are partitioned into indexed, oversized, failed, and cancelled categories.

Why this is the current recommended shape. Owned jobs move through channels; Arc is used only for shared cancellation and receiver ownership. Mutex scope covers dequeue, not file I/O. A pure streaming counter preserves state across reads, per-file status preserves partial failures, and final sorting makes entries deterministic.

Reasonable alternative and tradeoff. A work-stealing library is a reasonable alternative for CPU-heavy independent jobs and may simplify scheduling. The explicit fixed worker pool is a good fit here because its bounded queues and shutdown dependencies are the subject and are small enough to inspect. Unbounded thread-per-file spawning is a deliberate rejected design, not an early recommended step.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. Chunk-boundary counts; empty files; oversize and missing paths; cancellation before submission; queue-one termination; repeatable entries; invalid configuration. The total bound includes capped path/result metadata, not just the 8192-byte buffers. Ordinary file reads can block cancellation. Files may change during a run. Partial counts from failed or oversized files are not complete-file statistics.

Requirement that would justify evolution. For recursive or effectively unbounded discovery, stream results to a sink and use bounded or external sorting instead of collecting an unlimited list. For hard shutdown deadlines, revisit the synchronous I/O boundary and supported file types. For time-based or per-byte progress, define sampling and synchronization costs first; the present observer is per returned file and has no timing promise.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

title: Futures, waiting and cancellation
summary: Understand async state, polling and deadlines before composing a health monitor.
objectives: Distinguish creating a future from executing its work
Explain what state survives an await point
Understand why blocking work defeats cooperative deadlines
State what cancellation can and cannot undo
body:
Purpose: wait for sockets without dedicating a thread to each wait

Our indexer used synchronous reads and a fixed number of operating-system threads. The health monitor has a different workload: many small operations spend most of their time waiting for sockets. Async Rust represents those operations as futures that a runtime polls. When an operation cannot progress, it can arrange to be woken when progress may be possible. This permits many waiting operations to share a smaller set of executor threads. It does not automatically parallelize CPU-heavy code, remove ownership requirements, or make an arbitrary blocking function cancellable.

Model: a future is a suspended computation with owned state

An async function returns a future. Its body progresses when that future is polled, typically through await or spawning on a runtime. Values needed after a suspension point become part of the future's stored state. In P08, the socket and a bounded status-line buffer live across reads. The runtime can stop polling one future while another becomes ready. An await is a potential suspension point, not a promise that suspension always occurs. If the awaited operation is immediately ready, execution can continue without handing another task a turn.

Predict the deadline boundary

Imagine a request that connects successfully but never receives a response byte. A timeout wrapping only connect would not protect the read. A timeout wrapping the whole request covers connect, request write and status-line read together. Now imagine a CPU loop inside that future which never awaits. A cooperative runtime cannot force that loop to yield merely because a timer deadline passes. Before running the reference, mark the exact expression covered by attempt_timeout and the larger expression covered by endpoint_timeout. Include retry backoff in the latter budget.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo test -p p08-monitor hung_endpoint
mise exec -- cargo test -p p08-monitor retries_then_recovers
mise exec -- cargo run -p p08-monitor

The no-argument demo creates its own loopback listener on an operating-system-selected port and monitors that listener. It needs no internet service or credentials. Its exact socket address changes across runs. Predict the status and attempt count rather than memorizing a port number. The timeout test uses an accepted socket that deliberately never responds, so it tests a stalled read rather than only a failed connection.

Read the future composition

request performs one transport attempt and owns its TcpStream. probe loops over a bounded attempt count. Each attempt wraps request in timeout, converts transport and elapsed errors to explicit statuses, and stops after a healthy response. A separate timeout covers the full retry operation. tokio::select! races that operation against a cancellation future. When one branch completes, the losing future is dropped. Because request owns the socket, dropping it releases that local socket handle. Nothing in this structure says that bytes already transmitted are withdrawn or that a remote peer forgets the request.

Cancellation is a semantic decision

Canceling a read-only health probe is comparatively simple: the monitor abandons interest in a result and closes local work. Canceling a payment request or a database mutation would need a different story because remote side effects may already have occurred. Carry the uncertain-outcome lesson from storage into async programming. Dropping a future stops future polling of that computation; it does not travel backward in time. If a spawned task is detached by dropping only its handle, that task may continue. P08 retains task ownership in a JoinSet, aborts outstanding tasks on shutdown, and drains the set before returning.

The shutdown channel carries the latest boolean state. The cancellation helper checks the current value before waiting for changes, preventing an already-issued shutdown from being missed. A closed sender is also treated as cancellation so the monitor does not keep running without its owner. Be careful with borrowed watch values: a borrow guard should not accidentally be kept across an await. The reference checks the value in a short expression and then separately awaits change.

Intentional failure and guided checkpoint

In a disposable branch, move the timeout inside request so it wraps only TcpStream::connect. Run the hung-endpoint test under its outer three-second test guard. Predict the result before running. Restore the original request-wide timeout. This mutation experiment demonstrates the distinction between connection failure and a server that accepts but never answers. Your checkpoint is a diagram with nested boxes: per-attempt request, retry loop including backoff, endpoint total deadline, and monitor shutdown. Label which future owns each resource and which boundary drops it.

Playbook investigation: a timeout does not fire on time

Observation: a modified monitor returns much later than its configured timeout. Hypothesis A says Tokio's clock is broken. Hypothesis B says code blocks an executor thread or performs a long non-yielding loop. Hypothesis C says the timeout wraps only part of the operation. You choose the first experiment. One strong disproof of A is to run a timeout around a simple pending future in the same runtime and observe prompt completion. Then replace the suspect body with async sleep and compare. Inspect the placement of timeout separately so you do not conflate scheduling and coverage mistakes.

A fix may move blocking work to an appropriate bounded blocking facility or enlarge the timeout's lexical coverage. The evidence must show the stalled operation, not just an easy successful request. Its limits include scheduler delays and the fact that deadlines are cooperative rather than real-time guarantees. State what was canceled locally and what external side effects, if any, could already have happened.

Independent practice and tiered hints

Implement the scaffold's retry_budget using Duration arithmetic. Decide whether an exact zero remaining budget permits another attempt; the acceptance contract says it does not.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

Worked solution

Solution direction: reject exhausted attempt count, use checked_sub twice, reject zero, then take the smaller duration. Independently add a test for shutdown before any endpoint is spawned and another for sender closure. Compare the task counts with an in-flight shutdown case.

When you get stuck

Run one timeout test, draw its ownership boxes, and inspect which future the timeout actually receives. Read Future::poll and Tokio timeout documentation. Ask for review with the minimal stalled operation, the configured deadlines, whether the code yields, and the tasks still alive afterward. Avoid proposing a longer timeout until you know which boundary was exceeded.

Review and mastery

Submit the timeout-coverage mutation, the future ownership diagram and the retry arithmetic tests. Engineering decisions and evidence

Current scope and invariants. Only literal loopback endpoints are admitted. Input count, task count, attempts, status-line storage and deadlines are bounded. Every spawned task stays owned until joined or aborted and drained.
