Per-attempt and total deadlines cover different scopes, and a watch channel carries shutdown state. Results retain input indices so scheduling does not change report order. Controlled local listeners make failure tests reproducible.

Reasonable alternative and tradeoff. A maintained HTTP client is the appropriate choice when TLS, redirects, connection pooling, complete framing or real HTTP interoperability is required. The tiny status-line parser is a deliberately scoped transport exercise. A semaphore is useful for shared permits but would not by itself bound the number of spawned waiting tasks.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. 503 then healthy retry; malformed response; stalled read deadline; concurrency-one cap and input order; shutdown after a known acceptance signal; remote-address rejection. Cancellation stops local future work, not requests already sent. Aborted rows do not retain task-local attempt counts. Deadlines are cooperative rather than real-time guarantees. No TLS, redirects or response-body parser is implemented.

Requirement that would justify evolution. Replace the transport parser as soon as requirements exceed one bounded local status line. Add jitter, rate policy and observability only when operating requirements specify them. Accurate attempt counts for forcibly aborted tasks require explicit progress reporting.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

title: A bounded local health monitor
summary: Combine capped concurrency, layered deadlines, bounded retries and shutdown into one tested service client.
objectives: Bound spawned tasks as well as active socket operations
Test retries and deadlines with controlled loopback listeners
Preserve input order while tasks finish out of order
Terminate spawned work explicitly on shutdown
body:
Purpose: make a complete asynchronous tool

The finished P08 monitor performs one round over a finite list of literal loopback socket addresses. Each endpoint receives a bounded number of attempts, a timeout for each attempt and a timeout for the entire endpoint including backoff. The monitor caps how many endpoint tasks exist at once and returns rows in input order. Shutdown cancels outstanding work and waits for task cleanup. This is a teaching HTTP client: it reads a bounded status line, does not implement TLS or redirects, and does not parse general response bodies. Use an established HTTP client when those features become requirements.

Model: three budgets and one owner

The input budget allows at most 128 endpoints. The concurrency budget allows one through 32 endpoint tasks. The time budget limits each attempt and the total retry operation, while the attempt count is bounded independently. These limits protect different resources. A semaphore around the socket call would limit active connections but could still allow an unbounded number of waiting tasks if every endpoint were spawned upfront. P08 instead fills a JoinSet only to capacity, consumes a completion, then admits another endpoint. The monitor function remains the owner responsible for every spawned task.

Predict completion order and display order

Suppose endpoint A pauses before replying, B immediately returns 503 then 200, and C is healthy on its first attempt. With concurrency two, B may finish before A and permit C to start. The report still uses the original input order. Predict which facts should be stable across runs: addresses, final status under a controlled fixture, and bounded attempt counts. Exact durations and scheduling order need not be stable. A peak_in_flight value is instrumentation about admitted tasks, not proof of simultaneous CPU execution or a benchmark of networking performance.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo test -p p08-monitor
mise exec -- cargo run -p p08-monitor

Read admission, collection and shutdown

title: Measure a claim before optimizing
summary: Use a repeatable release-profile experiment and correctness oracle to evaluate performance changes.
objectives: Define the measured workload and timing boundary
Separate compiler profile, workload shape and algorithm effects
Collect multiple local measurements without inventing guarantees
Reject optimizations that change semantics or weaken validation
body:
Purpose: turn “faster” into a testable statement

Performance work begins with a question whose conditions are explicit. “The replay is fast” has no workload, machine, profile or correctness requirement. A useful claim might say that one implementation processes a fixed synthetic stream with identical resulting state in less elapsed time under a recorded release build. P12 provides a small benchmark executable so you can practice constructing that evidence. It reports measurements from your machine when you run it. This course does not supply invented throughput numbers or suggest that a toy stream predicts production market-system performance.

Model: measured time includes a chosen boundary

The benchmark compares immediate streaming with a reusable buffer holding at most 1024 events. Both timed regions include synthetic generation and complete replay, including creation of a fresh Replay and any batch allocation. The timer stops when the selected variant returns. Full-state comparison, digest calculation, output and final state destruction happen afterward. One untimed reference run supplies the expected state. Each variant receives two warm-ups and seven measured trials, with first/second order alternating within each pair rather than randomized. The executable prints raw TSV sample rows; the recorded measurement report computes minimum, median and maximum from those observations. If you change this boundary, label the new measurement rather than treating it as equivalent work.

Predict what will change

Before running, predict why the comparison requires a release build, what a tiny versus large event count changes, and how two live orders differ from thousands of live orders. Explain why the last comparison could change allocation and tree-lookup behavior even when total event count stays constant. Predict that the digest should remain stable for the same count and generator rule; do not predict a particular elapsed time. Background activity, CPU power state, thermal behavior and filesystem cache effects can affect observations. Repetition helps reveal variation but does not eliminate all confounding factors.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- rustc -Vv
mise exec -- cargo test -p p12-replay
mise exec -- cargo run --release -p p12-replay --bin benchmark -- 1000003

Read the harness before trusting its output

Argument parsing accepts an event count from one through ten million. The harness rejects a debug build so a profile mismatch cannot silently become comparative evidence. black_box discourages optimization based on visible inputs and outputs, but remains a best-effort barrier. require_same compares every completed Replay with the untimed reference, including orders, sequence, capacity and accounting. The printed digest is a convenient diagnostic, not the correctness gate. The batch-boundary regression also compares complete states at counts around 1024. These comparisons detect semantic divergence for the exercised inputs; they do not establish every possible workload or failure behavior.

Inspect the workload's hidden assumptions

The synthetic generator repeats two placements followed by their cancellations. Its live map never exceeds two orders. That is excellent for a bounded demonstration and poor evidence for lookup behavior in a large active book. Price values vary by a deterministic rule, and no network, exchange matching, latency distribution or real data feed is modeled. The benchmark includes allocation for inserted map entries, but its state-size distribution is unusually small. Record these facts beside each result. A performance conclusion should name this workload, not quietly generalize to all replay systems.

Intentional failure: make a misleading comparison

Run the comparative executable once without --release and predict its refusal before execution. That failure enforces the harness contract; it is not a Rust installation defect. Now review a fictional report comparing an old debug measurement with a new release measurement. The attribution is invalid because implementation and profile changed together. Repeat both real variants under one release profile and input count. Separately consider a “faster” implementation that skips duplicate-ID checks: run the rejection tests before interpreting its timing. Correctness is a constraint of the experiment, not a separate nice-to-have after optimization.

Playbook investigation: a claimed twofold improvement

You receive only a screenshot of one throughput figure and a patch replacing BTreeMap with another representation. Observations are incomplete: the screenshot does not establish event count, compiler version, profile, active-state size or whether validation still runs. Form at least three competing hypotheses. One may attribute improvement to the data structure, another to a release-profile change, and another to a smaller workload. Design a paired experiment that can disprove your favored explanation. For example, keep the old implementation but use the screenshot's build profile; if it improves similarly, the patch is not sufficient evidence for the claimed cause.

Choose the next investigation step independently. You might capture exact commands, inspect generated input counts, or compare complete resulting states. Do not begin by rewriting the program again. A defensible report includes raw observations, controls, at least one disproved hypothesis, and remaining uncertainty. A fix can be “correct the benchmark procedure and withdraw the unsupported claim.” Engineering progress does not always require a source-code change.

Guided checkpoint and independent practice

Write a measurement plan before execution: question, fixed inputs, build profile, timing boundary, correctness oracle, number of trials and environmental observations. Then add a second deterministic generator whose live set grows to a chosen bounded size before cancellations. Keep the original generator as a baseline. Independently evaluate one change such as reducing repeated lookups or adjusting representation. Preserve failure semantics, including unchanged state after rejection. Decide what variation would be too large to justify your conclusion and what additional experiment would resolve it.

Tiered hints and solution direction
Hint 1: choose the next observation

compare like with like before searching for an advanced profiler.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

event count and maximum live state are different workload dimensions.

Worked solution

A sound investigation first proves semantic equality on small adversarial streams, then repeats equivalent large workloads under one recorded profile. Retain rejected experiments in the log with the reason they were invalid. Do not select only the fastest trial as representative of normal behavior.

When you get stuck

Run the correctness tests, capture mise exec -- rustc -Vv, and read the benchmark's start and stop lines. Inspect std::hint::black_box's stated limitations. Ask for review with both commands, all reported samples, workload rule, digest and complete-state comparisons. “It feels slower” should become a reproducible observation before anyone proposes a low-level optimization.

Review, evidence and mastery

Submit the measurement plan, local output, a paired comparison and a limits paragraph. Mastery means making a causal claim no stronger than the experiment supports. You should be able to reject misleading evidence, preserve correctness while changing performance, and explain why a local median is useful without presenting it as a service-level guarantee or a prediction for an unrelated workload.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Current scope and invariants. The next sequence is exact, live order count is capped, fixed-point prices are validated, and rejected events preserve the entire replay state. All fallible accounting is checked before a placement is committed.

Why this is the current recommended shape. Newtypes separate event and order IDs; a private Price representation prevents invalid ticks entering through safe constructors. Replay accounting stays private behind read-only getters, so callers cannot bypass transition validation by assigning metrics. Integer arithmetic expresses the chosen scale exactly. A BTreeMap gives stable iteration, generators stream events, and full-state comparisons accompany digest checks.

Reasonable alternative and tradeoff. A hash map can offer different lookup costs, but deterministic output would need a separate ordering step and measurement on a representative workload. A mature decimal type is appropriate when varying scales or richer decimal operations become requirements. Neither abstraction is needed to express this fixed four-place bounded exercise clearly.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. Exact decimal grammar and limits; full-state deterministic replay; duplicate and sequence rejection; capacity and absent cancellation; injected accounting overflow; bounded generated live state. The supplied generator keeps only two live orders. A digest can collide and omits internal details; it is not an equivalence proof. Local benchmark samples include generation and exclude final digest/destruction. No universal timing claims are made.

Requirement that would justify evolution. Revisit representation and benchmark workload when active-state size, persistence, out-of-order arrival or domain rules expand. This is a state-transition exercise, not a matching engine. Add an amendment only after specifying its accounting and identity semantics.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

Patch verification: the coordinated targeted suite passed after adding P06 write-failure and stale-compaction regressions and making P12 accounting private. The exact execution is recorded in verification/patch001-targeted.log; independent review remains pending.

Recorded comparative evidence

The authored measurement report records the actual release-profile comparison: 1,000,003 events, two warm-ups and seven samples per variant, alternating pair order, and complete-state equality. The local streaming median was 8.805 ms and the bounded-batch median 9.574 ms. Batching was slower in all seven paired observations on that recorded workload; no CPU or allocator profile was collected to attribute the cause. The same report separately compares one and four indexer workers over a fixed warm-cache fixture. Preserve these workload and environment limits when discussing the observations.

title: Deterministic replay with exact domain values
summary: Model events, fixed-point prices and bounded state so the same accepted stream reproduces the same result.
objectives: Use distinct IDs and exact fixed-point prices
Validate before mutation so rejections are transactional

body:
Purpose: separate a domain state machine from its transport

P12 replays synthetic placement and cancellation events into a bounded map of resting orders. It is not an exchange simulator, matching engine, trading strategy or model of profitability. That narrow purpose lets us focus on exact representation, sequencing and failure semantics. The core API receives an Event and either accepts a transition or rejects it without changing state. A CLI generates a deterministic stream and prints the resulting summary. A separate benchmark measures that same core. Keeping generation, state transitions and measurement distinct makes it possible to test each claim without depending on a network feed.

Model: make invalid meanings harder to mix

OrderId and EventId are separate newtypes even though both wrap u64. An order identifier locates a live order; an event sequence identifies the required next transition. Mixing them is a semantic bug that primitive integers alone would not reveal. Price stores integer ticks at a scale of ten thousand, so 12.34 becomes exactly 123400 ticks. Decimal parsing checks grammar, precision and bounds using integer arithmetic. It rejects signs, exponents, non-digits, zero and excessive precision. Display reconstructs a four-place decimal string. This is a chosen domain scale, not a universal representation for every financial instrument.

Predict state and rejection behavior

Start with sequence one and place order seven. Submit sequence two with order seven again. Predict both the error and every state field afterward. The duplicate is rejected and the expected sequence remains two, allowing a corrected event with sequence two to be retried. Now cancel an absent order or exceed capacity. Those failures also leave state unchanged. Order IDs may be reused after their earlier order has been removed; the reference checks active duplicates rather than preserving a lifetime history of every ID. State this policy explicitly before extending the system.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo run -p p12-replay -- 100003
mise exec -- cargo test -p p12-replay rejection_is_transactional
mise exec -- cargo test -p p12-replay injected_accounting_overflow
mise exec -- cargo test --manifest-path scaffolds/p12-replay/Cargo.toml

Read the transition boundary

apply first compares the event sequence with next_sequence and computes checked increments. For a placement, it validates quantity, duplicate status and capacity, then checks the new accumulated notional before inserting. Only after the operation succeeds does it publish the next sequence and accepted count. The cancellation branch removes an existing order; removing a missing key changes nothing and returns an error. The test clones the whole Replay before a rejected event and compares the complete state afterward. That assertion is stronger than checking only the number of orders.

Exact arithmetic still needs overflow policy

Fixed-point integers avoid binary floating-point rounding for the chosen scale, but they do not make overflow impossible. Price and quantity have explicit limits. Their product is accumulated in u128 with checked_add. The submitted_notional_ticks field is a sum of submitted values, not executed volume or profit. The overflow test deliberately sets internal accounting to its maximum and attempts another placement. It asserts that overflow rejects the event without partially inserting the order or advancing sequence. This is failure injection aimed at a real boundary, even though the ordinary small synthetic workload will not approach it.

Determinism includes ordering and inputs

The map is a BTreeMap, so iteration uses a defined key order. The generator derives every event from its index and does not read wall-clock time or random operating-system state. The core uses no concurrent mutation, floating-point accumulation or external I/O. Those choices make identical input streams produce identical full states under the stated semantics. The digest summarizes accepted count, notional and sorted live orders using a stable byte order, but it can collide and does not include every internal field. Use full equality for correctness tests and treat the digest as a convenient quick check.

Playbook investigation: equal digests, unequal behavior

You receive a report saying two implementations are equivalent because their benchmark digests match. The report omits rejection behavior and uses a count divisible by four, which leaves no active orders. Observations are therefore weaker than the conclusion. Propose competing hypotheses: both implementations are correct, one skips an invalid transition, or the workload fails to exercise the changed path. Construct a short stream ending with live orders and include duplicate, missing-cancel and out-of-order events. If either implementation changes state after rejection, that disproves equivalence even if the original benchmark digest matched.

Choose another disproof experiment independently. One option is comparing complete state after every accepted prefix rather than only the final empty map. Another is changing an exact price by one tick and following its contribution through accounting. Record the earliest divergent transition so the investigation targets a small cause. The fix should restore the specified transition semantics and add a regression at that boundary; changing the digest until outputs match would merely hide the symptom.

Guided checkpoint and independent practice

Complete the scaffold's price parser without converting through f64. Write a grammar table showing accepted and rejected inputs, including the maximum price and an overflowing decimal string. Then add an amendment event to your own replay implementation. Decide whether an amendment keeps order identity, how it affects accounting, and what happens when quantity is invalid. Write the before/after contract before code. Preserve atomic rejection with a candidate value or complete validation before mutation. A reproducible run starts with an exact CLI contract

The replay command accepts zero arguments for 100003 generated events, or exactly one event count parsed as usize. The count therefore fits this target's pointer-sized unsigned integer; it is not a floating-point quantity. Extra arguments are rejected. Previously, reading only nth(1) let 3 extra silently run three events, which could hide a mistyped benchmark or reproducibility command. The corrected parser checks arity before any replay work and handles non-UTF-8 text as an input error rather than panicking.

Apply the playbook: hypothesis A says an extra token changes the generated stream; hypothesis B says the parser never inspects it. The before-fix process test observed successful output for 3 extra, and source inspection identified the missing read. After the fix, the same request reports input failure with no replay output, while 3 still reports exactly three events. Run mise exec -- cargo test --manifest-path projects/Cargo.toml -p p12-replay --test cli from the course root. The test demonstrates an input-boundary correction, not faster replay or stronger event semantics.

Before reading the adapter below, propose a separate file-input mode and define its grammar, size limits, ownership and failure behavior before extending this parser. Do not treat a native file path as UTF-8 protocol text. The companion benchmark already validates all arguments and applies its own 1..=10000000 measurement budget. See the before/after evidence and the version-matched argument documentation.

Output is an I/O boundary too. The CLI writes through a locked io::Write handle and propagates ordinary stdout failures, including a pipe whose consumer has closed. Final stderr diagnostics are best effort: a second write failure must not replace the original failure with a panic. The process tests create an anonymous pipe and close its reading end before launching the child, so this experiment does not depend on a race with a shell command.

Read synthetic tick files through a bounded pipeline

The generated order-state exercise above isolates transition costs. Now cross a real file boundary. A tick here is one synthetic observed price and quantity, not an order instruction or an execution. Its output is a per-symbol summary. Keeping the tick adapter separate avoids pretending that the previous place/cancel events were market-data rows. Both remain local, reproducible exercises with no broker, credentials or live market connection.

Write the schema before the parser

The first line must be exactly event_id,timestamp_ms,symbol,price,quantity. Every data row has exactly five comma-separated fields. This deliberately narrow format has no quoted fields, comments, embedded commas, spaces or byte-order mark. LF and CRLF line endings are accepted; the final line may omit its terminator. A blank data row is an error, while a header with no rows is a valid empty replay. The file is UTF-8 even though its filesystem path remains a native operating-system path.

  • event_id: decimal digits parsed as u64. The first accepted ID is 1; each next ID must increase by exactly one. Duplicate, missing, zero and out-of-order IDs are rejected. This is rejection, not deduplication or reordering.
  • timestamp_ms: nonnegative u64 milliseconds since the Unix epoch in this synthetic data model. Values cannot move backwards. Equal timestamps are ordered by event ID. We do not convert these integers into calendar dates, consult a wall clock, infer exchange timing or claim to validate real feeds.
  • symbol: one through twelve ASCII uppercase letters. At most 64 distinct symbols are accepted by default.
  • price: positive ordinary decimal text with at most four fractional digits, at most 100000000.0000. No sign, exponent or bare trailing decimal point is accepted. Existing Price stores units of 1/10000 exactly.
  • quantity: decimal digits in 1..=1000000. It counts synthetic units. Notional is the exact sum of price ticks times quantity, not money earned or a trading return.

Every line is limited to 256 bytes including its LF or CRLF terminator. The default event budget is 1000000 and can be lowered through the library. Batches hold at most 1024 parsed ticks; the default is 64. The file CLI uses a 4096-byte input buffer. Count, volume and notional additions use checked arithmetic even though the present input limits keep valid totals well below the integer maxima.

Predict and run the supplied fixture

Before running, calculate ALFA's total volume and notional from these rows. Will changing the batch size from one to two change its first/last price? Does BETA's timestamp tie with ALFA require sorting? Write the expected result first.

cd rust-course
mise exec -- cargo run --locked --manifest-path projects/Cargo.toml -p p12-replay --bin tick_replay -- projects/reference/p12-replay/fixtures/ticks.csv 2
mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path projects/Cargo.toml -p p12-replay --all-targets

Working directory: the portable course root after the first command; omit that cd if already there. The output is labeled SIMULATED TICKS. It reports five events, ALFA volume 7 and notional 6992500 ticks, and BETA volume 5 and notional 2505000 ticks. ALFA first/last/low/high prices are 100.0000, 99.5000, 99.5000 and 101.2500. Batch sizes 1, 2, 64 and 1024 produce byte-identical fixture output in the executed process tests.

Follow each boundary in the implementation

Limits::validate prevents zero or excessive budgets before reading. line wraps the reader in Read::take before calling read_until; a newline-free input can therefore supply at most 257 retained bytes to this operation before rejection. Checking length only after an unrestricted read_until would permit unbounded growth. This bound concerns retained input bytes; allocator capacity, metadata and operating-system buffering are not an exact RAM measurement.

parse validates the field count and each type before constructing a private Tick. The symbol becomes owned because its tick must survive reuse of the line buffer. This is a justified small ownership transfer. A borrowed symbol would require retaining the owning line across the batch, making that ownership structure more complex without serving this scope.

replay fills one reusable vector and drains it in input order into Summary::apply. Draining preserves vector capacity. This is a synchronous staged pipeline: the producer stops reading whenever the batch is full, and there are no channels or spawned tasks. It bounds work retained between ingestion and aggregation without claiming parallel speed. The BTreeMap limits state to the admitted symbols and gives deterministic sorted report order. For N events, B batch capacity and S symbols, retained domain state is O(B + S), and aggregation is O(N log S), plus reading and bounded parsing work.

apply checks the next ID, timestamp and symbol budget, computes a prospective aggregate with checked arithmetic, and only then mutates the map and counters. A rejected event leaves that summary unchanged. The public file replay returns either a whole successful summary or an error; the CLI prints no successful partial summary after an input error. It may have read and processed a prefix internally. Because batch parsing and application are distinct stages, malformed files can reveal different first diagnostics at different batch sizes; the contract promises rejection, not a batch-independent choice among multiple defects.

First and last refer to event order for that symbol. Low and high compare integer price ticks. A volume-weighted average would be the rational value notional_ticks / volume, still expressed in price ticks. This adapter retains the exact numerator and denominator rather than silently rounding a display value. A future display needs an explicit rounding rule.

Guided project checkpoint

Reconstruct a fresh final source copy from the course root. Read fixtures/ticks.csv, then trace header, bounded line, field conversion, bounded batch, summary and output in that order. Run the commands before changing the fixture. The helper refuses an existing destination.

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p12 final --destination learner-work/tick-investigation
mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path learner-work/tick-investigation/Cargo.toml --all-targets
mise exec -- cargo run --locked --manifest-path learner-work/tick-investigation/Cargo.toml --bin tick_replay -- learner-work/tick-investigation/fixtures/ticks.csv 2

The preserved default binary remains the generated order replay, so existing cargo run -- 3 commands still work. No dependency or lockfile resolution change was needed. The reconstructed final checkpoint was compiled and tested independently, including both binaries.

Deliberate mistake and playbook investigation

In the learner copy only, duplicate row 2. The intended result is a sequence error, not double-counted volume. Hypothesis A says equal timestamps make duplicates legitimate; hypothesis B says event identity controls admission independently of time. The original fixture already has tied timestamps and succeeds, while the duplicated ID is rejected. That comparison disproves A. Sorting rows by timestamp would hide neither a duplicate identity nor a gap, and silently dropping repeats would introduce a new idempotency contract the exercise has not specified.

The worked regression constructs one accepted tick and then tries a duplicate, a skipped ID, a backwards timestamp and a second symbol beyond a lowered limit. It compares the entire summary after every rejection. Separate fault-injection cases set internal counters near overflow and verify no partial mutation. Those injected states are intentionally outside normal bounded input; they exercise defensive arithmetic branches, not a claim that valid fixtures can reach them.

Independent practice and progressively revealed review

Add a VWAP display with an explicit tie-breaking rounding rule. Specify what happens for an empty replay. Then design, without implementing immediately, a deduplication policy that distinguishes an identical retried event from a conflicting event using the same ID. State how much history it retains and what happens after that history expires. Finally investigate whether batch size helps this file workload before changing its default.

Hint 1: keep domain arithmetic exact

Divide the integer notional by volume only at the display boundary. The remainder contains the information needed to decide rounding. Empty input has no symbol aggregate and therefore no VWAP.

Hint 2: identity is not payload equality

A set of IDs can reject repeats but cannot explain whether a repeated ID carries a changed symbol, price or quantity. Define conflict behavior before choosing retained data.

Reference reasoning

For a four-place display, compute quotient and remainder in price ticks. For round-half-up, increment the quotient when twice the remainder is at least the volume; use checked or sufficiently wide arithmetic and state that this differs from half-even. Return no value for zero volume. A bounded deduplication window requires a retained ID-to-content representation and a policy for older repeats; a digest alone adds a collision assumption. Benchmark equivalent successful inputs in release mode, compare complete aggregates and retain all samples. Larger batches add temporary owned values and may not improve throughput in a synchronous pipeline.

When you get stuck

Read the reported line and reduce the file to its header plus the smallest prefix that still fails. Keep event IDs and the intended timestamp policy in the report. Compare batch=1 with the failing batch size to locate parsing versus state transition, then inspect the test that challenges that boundary. Ask for review with the fixture bytes, expected full aggregate, exact command, actual error and one competing hypothesis. Do not request an optimization before confirming identical semantics.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The standard library and the existing exact Price type suffice for this restricted format. A maintained CSV parser would be appropriate if quoted fields or broad CSV interoperability were required; it would still need an outer byte budget. Concurrent stages would require a measured bottleneck plus explicit queue, cancellation and task-ownership policies. Sorting an unbounded file would violate this adapter's retained-state contract; supporting out-of-order ticks needs a defined bounded reorder window or external storage.

The tests cover exact aggregates, batch boundary equivalence, grammar, CRLF and final-line behavior, row/budget rejection, duplicate and out-of-order IDs, backwards timestamps, unchanged state on rejected events, checked-overflow injection, an infinite newline-free reader, I/O failure, and a generated 20000-row stream that does not retain the file. This is evidence for the concrete resource design and invariants, not a measured RSS bound or tick-throughput claim. The existing order-event benchmark still measures its original generated workload; it does not measure CSV ingestion. See executed commands and limits. Mastery requires explaining the order/identity/time distinction, making a justified schema change, preserving rejected-state invariants and producing your own reproducible investigation.

title: A small unsafe boundary with explicit invariants
summary: Build and audit fixed-capacity storage while keeping a safe implementation as the behavioral baseline.
objectives: Describe initialized storage separately from allocated storage
Justify each unsafe operation locally
Preserve ownership, bounds, alignment and aliasing through a safe API
Test drop behavior, zero-sized values and panic paths without claiming proof
body:
Purpose: understand the responsibility unsafe introduces

Unsafe Rust permits operations whose safety preconditions the compiler cannot fully verify at that location. It does not turn off ownership checking everywhere, and it is not an optimization badge. P13 implements a tiny fixed-capacity stack to make those preconditions visible. The public API is safe: callers can push, pop, borrow live elements and clear the stack. Internally, an array of MaybeUninit holds storage that may or may not contain initialized T values. A heap-backed SafeSlots implementation provides the same basic capacity behavior without unsafe code. Start with that safe baseline before evaluating whether the low-level representation is worth its audit cost.

Model: allocation and initialization are different facts

FixedSlots owns N storage slots and a length. The central invariant is that len is at most N and exactly the half-open prefix 0..len contains live initialized values; the index len is excluded. The remaining storage is not exposed as T. Storage availability does not establish initialization: reading an uninitialized integer, reference or other value can violate Rust's validity rules. MaybeUninit provides a way to hold such storage without pretending it already contains a T. The fields stay private so safe callers cannot increase len or overwrite the representation behind the API's reasoning.

Predict ownership at full and empty boundaries

Push two owned Strings into a capacity-two stack, then push a third. Predict who owns the rejected String. The API returns Err(value), preserving ownership rather than dropping it unexpectedly or writing beyond capacity. Pop transfers ownership of the final live value and shrinks the initialized prefix. An empty pop returns None. For capacity zero, every push returns its value. For a zero-sized type, several logical elements may occupy no distinct bytes, but their count and destructors still matter. Treat these as primary cases, not exotic afterthoughts.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo run -p p13-unsafe
mise exec -- cargo test -p p13-unsafe
mise exec -- rustc --edition=2024 ../exercises/systems/uninit_read.rs
mise exec -- cargo test --manifest-path scaffolds/p13-unsafe/Cargo.toml

The rustc command intentionally fails with E0133 because assume_init_read requires an explicit unsafe block even though this particular slot was initialized. The compiler requires the caller to take responsibility for that operation's preconditions. Adding the block without checking those preconditions would silence a diagnostic without establishing safety.

Read each transition as an invariant proof obligation

push checks capacity, writes the new value, then increments len. Publishing length before initialization would let another path treat unwritten storage as live. pop decrements len before assume_init_read transfers the value out, preventing later cleanup from dropping it again. as_slice constructs a slice only over the initialized prefix. Its justification includes layout compatibility, alignment, one-array bounds, valid values and a lifetime tied to the borrow of self. as_mut_slice additionally relies on exclusive access through &mut self. The unsafe comments explain these facts at the operation that needs them.

Aliasing and lifetimes remain part of the safe interface

A shared slice returned by as_slice keeps the stack borrowed. Safe code cannot mutate the stack while that slice remains in use. The mutable slice likewise gives exclusive access for its borrow lifetime. The implementation must not manufacture a longer lifetime, expose uninitialized suffix storage, or allow mutation through a shared reference. No manual Send or Sync implementation is needed here; the compiler derives those properties from the fields when appropriate. Introducing raw-pointer caches or interior mutability later would require revisiting that reasoning rather than assuming the existing audit still applies.

Playbook investigation: tests pass, but is the wrapper safe?

You are shown a patch that changes as_slice to use N instead of len and a test screenshot showing successful push/pop of two u32 values in capacity two. The evidence omits partially filled storage. Hypothesis A says all allocated slots are valid values. Hypothesis B says the test only covered the fully initialized case. Hypothesis C says zero bytes happen to resemble valid u32 values on that run. Construct a test that borrows after one push into capacity two, but do not rely on ordinary execution to diagnose undefined behavior. The required reasoning already disproves A: allocation alone does not initialize T.

Restore the initialized-prefix length and review every path that changes it. Then compare the wrapper against the safe baseline across many deterministic push/pop operations, including non-Copy values. Tests support the audit by exploring behavior; they do not replace the invariant argument. Optional Miri checking uses a separately selected nightly toolchain through the course's mise workflow. It may catch invalid memory behavior on executed paths, but a pass is not a proof for every T, capacity and future code change.

Guided checkpoint and independent practice

Complete the scaffold while it forbids unsafe code. Preserve it as your oracle. Then annotate the reference with a table: operation, required invariant, temporary state and restored invariant. Independently add a safe get_mut method that reuses the established mutable-slice boundary rather than adding another raw-pointer operation. Explain why an index equal to len returns None. Extend tests to capacity zero, a type with alignment 64, and a zero-sized type whose Drop increments a counter. Leave performance claims out unless you conduct a separate controlled measurement.

Tiered hints and solution reasoning
Hint 1: choose the next observation

a smaller unsafe surface is easier to audit than repeated pointer arithmetic.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

existing slice methods already implement checked indexing.

Worked solution

Solution direction: get_mut can call as_mut_slice().get_mut(index). This adds safe composition without new unsafe obligations. For the initialized-prefix table, distinguish moving a value out with assume_init_read from borrowing it; the former must remove it from the set of values the container later drops.

When you get stuck

Stop at the first unsafe block whose preconditions you cannot state. Read MaybeUninit's initialization invariant and from_raw_parts_mut's safety section. Run only the corresponding boundary test. Ask for review with the invariant table, the exact unsafe expression, supported T assumptions and a minimal counterexample candidate. Do not ask a reviewer to certify soundness from a green test summary alone.

Review, evidence and mastery

Submit the safe baseline, invariant table, edge tests and an explicit statement of unverified assumptions. Mastery means recognizing when safe code is sufficient and, when unsafe code remains, explaining why every safe caller must still receive memory-safe behavior. This educational implementation is material for an audit, not an unsupported universal soundness claim.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Current scope and invariants. len never exceeds capacity; precisely the prefix below len contains owned initialized values. Borrowed slices expose only that prefix with self-tied lifetimes and appropriate exclusivity. A moved-out value is excluded from later cleanup.

Why this is the current recommended shape. A safe Vec-based model comes first. The compact unsafe representation uses private MaybeUninit storage, capacity checks before writes, initialization before length publication, and length removal before move-out. clear publishes empty state before user Drop code. Every unsafe expression has a local justification.

Reasonable alternative and tradeoff. A Vec or an established fixed-capacity collection is the preferred general application choice when its contract meets requirements. This custom wrapper is appropriate only for studying a small auditable boundary; no speed advantage or universal soundness proof is claimed. Adding more operations increases the audit surface and should be justified by an actual requirement.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. Zero capacity; bounds and ownership on full push; deterministic comparison with safe baseline; exactly-once non-Copy destruction; ZST counts and destructors; over-alignment; one caught destructor panic with reuse. Passing native tests or Miri is evidence for executed cases, not a universal soundness proof. A second panic while unwinding can abort. Independent review remains pending; author self-review cannot grant acceptance.

Requirement that would justify evolution. Use an established collection for production needs unless stack storage or another measured requirement justifies ownership of an unsafe implementation. Any new removal, iteration, interior-mutability or raw-pointer feature requires a renewed invariant review.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

Executed dynamic evidence: the course author ran the seven P13 tests under Miri using nightly-2026-10-08 through mise; all seven passed. See the course verification record for the exact command and log. This is author verification of executed paths, not independent acceptance or a universal soundness proof.

Safety contract: byte extent and what tests establish

The Rust 1.99.1 slice-construction contract also requires the total byte extent to fit within isize::MAX and its address calculation not to wrap. The pointer here comes from one live array object, and the private length stays within that array. A prefix therefore stays within that object's valid allocation extent; zero-sized elements have zero byte extent but still require an aligned, non-null pointer. State this argument alongside initialization, aliasing, and lifetime obligations. Adding a debug assertion alone would not establish the safe interface's contract.

Boundary tests demonstrate their chosen executions. The invariant argument must account for every permitted safe caller, and independent review remains separate. The earlier follow-up audit checked the installed Rust 1.99.0 primary documentation locally, reviewed all four unsafe sites, and reused the existing native, optimized, and Miri evidence; it does not claim a new universal soundness proof. See the narrow boundary audit.

title: Audit cleanup, panics and evidence limits
summary: Review the unsafe wrapper as a state machine, including destructor panics and zero-sized elements.
objectives: Explain cleanup ordering when user destructors panic
Distinguish leaks, double drops and invalid references
Use differential tests and dynamic checking as evidence with limits
Write a review that separates observed behavior from unproved claims
body:
Purpose: inspect the path that ordinary examples avoid

A container can behave correctly for integers and still mishandle owned resources, zero-sized values or a destructor that panics. An unsafe audit must consider every safe caller permitted by the API, not only the sample main function. P13 therefore includes exactly-once drop tests, over-aligned values, zero-sized values with destructors, repeated operations against a safe baseline and a single destructor panic during clear. This lesson asks you to evaluate what those tests establish, what the invariant argument establishes, and which questions remain. Reviewing is a distinct activity from authoring; a self-review does not become independent acceptance because the tests pass.

Model: cleanup is another state transition

clear first replaces len with zero and remembers the old length. It then asks slice drop glue to drop the old initialized prefix. Publishing the empty state before invoking user Drop code matters because a destructor can panic. If control later returns through catch_unwind and the container is dropped again, len zero prevents a second drop of those values. Slice drop glue handles cleanup of remaining elements during unwinding from a single element destructor panic. If another destructor panics while unwinding, the process may abort. The container cannot promise recovery from every sequence of panicking destructors or from a panic-abort build.

Predict three different failures

Predict what happens if pop reads a value without shrinking len, if clear shrinks len but forgets to drop the old prefix, and if as_slice exposes the uninitialized suffix. These are not equivalent mistakes. The first can cause duplicate ownership and double drop. The second can leak resources while remaining memory-safe under the relevant assumptions. The third can construct references to invalid values and cause undefined behavior. A review that labels all three “memory leak” loses the distinctions needed to choose tests and repairs. Write the invariant each mutation violates before running any deliberately broken version.

cd rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo test -p p13-unsafe values_are_dropped
mise exec -- cargo test -p p13-unsafe zero_sized_destructors
mise exec -- cargo test -p p13-unsafe a_single_destructor_panic -- --nocapture
mise exec -- cargo test -p p13-unsafe agrees_with_safe_baseline

The panic test intentionally triggers a destructor panic inside catch_unwind. The panic hook may print a message even though the test succeeds after checking recovery. Do not interpret the printed word “panic” alone as a failed test. Inspect the exit status and final assertions. Conversely, a caught panic is not evidence that arbitrary undefined behavior would be safely caught; those are fundamentally different failure categories.

Read the audit tests as experiments

The owned-value test shares a counter through Rc<Cell<usize>> on one test thread. It fills the container, receives a rejected value, drops that returned value, pops another and finally drops the container. Each step predicts an exact count. The zero-sized destructor test uses logical element count rather than pointer differences. The alignment test checks a deliberately over-aligned type. The differential test follows a deterministic operation sequence and compares the live slice with SafeSlots after every step. None of these requires exposing the private representation to ordinary callers.

Dynamic tools find counterexamples, not universal proofs

Miri can execute Rust code under an interpreter that checks many forms of undefined behavior. Use it as an additional investigation tool when an isolated nightly toolchain with the Miri component is available. Follow the course's opt-in mise instructions and record the exact nightly version, command and result; do not silently change the stable course pin or global default. If Miri is unavailable, mark the check not run rather than implying it passed. Even a clean run explores only the executed tests and the tool's model. The safety argument still has to cover untested capacities, valid types and permitted call sequences.

Playbook investigation: a red panic log and a green suite

You receive incomplete evidence: a screenshot containing “injected destructor panic,” a green summary, and a patch moving len=0 after drop_in_place. Hypothesis A says the test harness ignored a real failure. Hypothesis B says the expected panic was caught and assertions passed in the old version. Hypothesis C says the patch creates a double-drop risk only when clear unwinds. Reproduce the exact test command, inspect catch_unwind and track len at the unwind boundary. A passing test with the original ordering disproves the claim that every printed panic necessarily means test failure. It does not justify the patch.

Investigate the changed ordering without assuming ordinary execution will reliably expose invalid behavior. Reason from the state transition: if a destructor panics before len is cleared, later container cleanup can revisit already-dropped values. Restore empty-state publication before calling user destructors. Evidence includes drop counts, empty reusable storage after one caught panic, and a reviewed invariant trace. Its limits explicitly exclude survival from a second panic during unwinding and do not equate resource-leak freedom with all aspects of memory safety.

Guided checkpoint: perform a review without rewriting first

For each unsafe block, record the pointer origin, alignment, initialized range, exclusivity, lifetime and cleanup obligations that apply. Mark any obligation irrelevant to that particular operation instead of pasting the same checklist blindly. Trace new, successful push, rejected push, pop, borrowed slices, clear and Drop. Then inspect every early return and possible user-code invocation. You may discover that the smallest helpful change is a clearer invariant comment or a missing regression rather than a new abstraction. Review claims and evidence before changing implementation.

Independent practice and tiered hints

Design an additional adversarial operation sequence that is not identical to the existing deterministic loop. Include a clear followed by reuse and a non-Copy value. Decide whether to add a clear operation to the safe baseline or compare with a plain Vec model.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

the oracle should express expected behavior independently of raw storage.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

Worked solution

Solution direction: use tagged values with shared drop counters, retain popped values outside the container, and assert that clearing drops only values still owned by the container. Explain how your test could miss a lifetime bug even while those counts are correct.

When you get stuck

Reduce the audit to one transition and one owned value. Read MaybeUninit::assume_init_read and ptr::drop_in_place safety requirements, then rerun the matching test. For an optional Miri failure, include its exact toolchain and complete first diagnostic. Ask for review with a proposed counterexample, not a request to “approve unsafe.” Separate a confirmed defect, an unsupported concern and a check you have not run.

Evidence, independent review and mastery

Submit a review record with findings, severity based on actual violated obligations, reproductions, fixes, regression evidence and remaining limits. Mark author self-review separately from independent review. You have mastered this stage when you can challenge misleading evidence, explain cleanup under panic, and make a narrow justified conclusion without claiming that extensive tests or a dynamic checker mathematically prove soundness.

Adding more operations increases the audit surface and should be justified by an actual requirement.

Evidence and limits. Native reference tests were run through mise in the coordinated course verification; inspect the current verification record for exact results. Passing native tests or Miri is evidence for executed cases, not a universal soundness proof. A second panic while unwinding can abort. Independent review remains pending; author self-review cannot grant acceptance.

Requirement that would justify evolution. Use an established collection for production needs unless stack storage or another measured requirement justifies ownership of an unsafe implementation. Any new removal, iteration, interior-mutability or raw-pointer feature requires a renewed invariant review.

In your review, explain this choice in your own words, preserve the behavioral contract during changes, and name the evidence that would make you choose the alternative. Deliberately broken variants above are diagnostic exercises, never recommended implementation stages.

Optional isolated Miri check through mise

This opt-in path uses a dated nightly separately from the course's stable pin. Installing a toolchain and component changes local tool availability but does not change the global default. Run from rust-course/projects only when you choose to install the optional tools. A successful check covers the executed tests under Miri; it does not establish universal soundness.

mise install rust@nightly-2026-10-17
mise exec rust@nightly-2026-10-17 -- rustup component add miri --toolchain nightly-2026-10-17
mise exec rust@nightly-2026-10-17 -- cargo miri test -p p13-unsafe

Executed dynamic evidence: the course author ran the seven P13 tests under Miri using nightly-2026-10-08 through mise; all seven passed. See the course verification record for the exact command and log. This is author verification of executed paths, not independent acceptance or a universal soundness proof.

Safety contract: byte extent and what tests establish

The Rust 1.99.1 slice-construction contract also requires the total byte extent to fit within isize::MAX and its address calculation not to wrap. The pointer here comes from one live array object, and the private length stays within that array. A prefix therefore stays within that object's valid allocation extent; zero-sized elements have zero byte extent but still require an aligned, non-null pointer. Boundary tests demonstrate their chosen executions. The invariant argument must account for every permitted safe caller, and independent review remains separate. The earlier follow-up audit checked the installed Rust 1.99.0 primary documentation locally, reviewed all four unsafe sites, and reused the existing native, optimized, and Miri evidence; it does not claim a new universal soundness proof. See the narrow boundary audit.

Ownership transfer is different from leaking

The Rust 1.99 release guidance discourages reclaiming allocations after Box::leak. When a foreign API must eventually return ownership, begin with Box::into_raw or Box::into_non_null and reconstruct exactly once under their documented safety preconditions. An ordinary Box remains the simpler choice when Rust can retain ownership throughout. P13 does not leak and reclaim allocations.
